In addition to that what do we find? We find the department of the ex-Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) being criticised by hon. members opposite. Mr. Pelletier has given the most progressive and advanced legislation in connection with the Post Office Department of any man who has occupied that position in Canada. He has established a system of rural free mail delivery whereby the people living in the rural districts have the benefits of a post office at their very doors. The late Government for eight long years were urged to establish that system; but when they finally did undertake it they gave free rural delivery only on *existing mail and stage routes instead of in the extensive way that the late Postmaster General has established that system. Mr. Pelletier also gave to the people of Canada a parcel post system which will develop and grow as years go by. The policy of the Post Office Department under the Conservative Government has been progressive, advanced and in the interests of the country.
The hon. member for St. John referred in a very slight way to the reciprocity pact, calling attention to the wheat that would be going into the United States to-day if we had had reciprocity. If that hon. gentleman would read the papers and look at the columns showing the prices which are being paid for wheat in Winnipeg and Minneapolis, he would find that day after day and month after month and year after year the price in Winnipeg exceeds the price paid in Minneapolis. How can he believe that farmers are anxious to send their wheat over there at the present time when they are receiving in Canada a higher price than they could possibly receive on the other side of the line? Does he not realize that the people of the United States last year were able to export to the markets of the world 173,861,000 bushels of wheat and more tnan 12,000,000 barrels of flour, while this country was able to export only a very small portion of that amount. Which shows that the United States are capable of producing enough wheat' and flour to supply not only their own people but the people of other lands.	.
Our people have been anxious to promote the made-in-Canada campaign. Hon. gentlemen opposite do not seem to appreciate [Mr. J. E. Armstrong:.!
this made-in-Canada proposition. The hon. junior member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) called attention to it, and tried to lead the members of the House to believe that it was not to their best interests to urge upon the people of Canada to make and to consume as much of the products of their own land as possible. Do not these hon, gentlemen realize that the best market is the home market, and that the made-in-Canada proposition is a live and progressive idea, and that people in Canada should gladly and willingly support it?
Do these gentlemen want us to call attention to the position in which they were placed in 1911 when they voted against the three dreadnoughts that should to-day be in the firing line of the British fleet?
They would not have been completed until next year.

The ex-Minister of Public Works criticises this Government in its management of the affairs of Canada. Had these two battleships been completed and were to-day in the firing line of the British fleet, how proud the people of Canada would be. Does the hon. member for St. John not appreciate the fact that on the 5th day of August, when war was declared, the people of Canada were humiliated to think that they had done so little to aid the British Empire. Thousands of men in Canada hung their heads in shame to think they were unable to assist the Motherland in her defence. Who was to blame? Day in and day out, night in and night out, this Government did their utmost to carry this proposition through this House, so that assistance would be granted to the Motherland. They were doing just what the British Admiralty asked them to do. Any man who will read the memorandum that was placed before this Government in 1911 will realize that this Government was merely carrying out the wishes of the British Admiralty when they said that the best means whereby the Canadian people could assist the Motherland in the defence of the Empire would be by building three of the largest and best battleships that money could buy or science procure. The is the statement made in the memorandum, and the hon. gentlemen opposite did their ulmost to defeat that proposition.

The hon. gentleman says if these battleships had been completed Canada would have been proud of them. Did not the right hon. the Prime Minister, at the time when it was proposed to build them, say that they would not be completed

until after 1916? It would be after the general election; that would take place before they were completed.
That statement may have been made by the Premier of Canada.
No, it was not.
Yes, it was made distinctly and positively.

But supposing that it was made, under the present circumstances if those two battleships had been in the dockyards of England in process of construction, men could have been put to work on them night and day during the last seven months, we are not so far from the year 1916 that we cannot appreciate the fact that the British Admiralty would have been able to have completed those two battleships, and that to-day they might have been in the firing line of the British fleet.
Why didn't you have the Niobe ready?

Let me call attention to the fact that the people of Canada have looked on with admiration at the splendid fight put up by the warship furnished to the British Admiralty by the Government of New Zealand in the battle off Heligoland.
What about the Australian Government's boat?

And more than that, they were able to assist Admiral Beatty in the splendid victory he achieved in the North Sea. The cry with these gentlemen opposite was: "No need; no danger, no emergency; no menace; we know what we are talking about and there is no need for the Government to undertake this proposition." But the Premier had asked the British Admiralty how he could best serve them in that regard, and he is asking them to-day. This Government to-day are carrying out the wishes of the British Admiralty, and we are"proud and glad to support them. But hon. gentlemen opposite are doing their utmost to discredit this Government in the eyes of Canada and the world at large, and if possible drive them to the country. We on this side of the House are glad that we have at the head of affairs in Canada such an honest, straight-forward, and businesslike Governement, a Government which from time time to time gives to the people of Canada legislation as progressive as could possibly be expected from any Government. .

When the House rose at six o'clock I was calling attention to the fact that had this Government obeyed the wishes of the British Admiralty in 1911 and, had their policy not been thwarted in this House and defeated in the Senate by the Liberal party, Canada and Great Britain would to-day have been much better prepared for this war. Upon the shoulders of hon. gentlemen opposite, therefore, rests a great responsibility, and when called upon to give an account of their stewardship in the near future, they will cut a sorry figure before the people, when they have to tell them that their policy in this House so far this session has been) to embarrass and hinder the Government in promoting the necessary legislation to help the Empire to bring this great struggle to a successful issue. When war broke out we had no great dreadnoughts to place in the firing line, and for that hon. gentlemen opposite are to blame. They do not dare to vote in opposition to the $100,000,000 asked for by the Government now, nor did they dare to vote last summer against the $50,000,000 for war expenditure, but they do dare to try to embarrass and obstruct and criticise necessary legislation. The Government now in power has done its full duty in this crisis. One hundred thousand of our brave soldiers have been armed and equipped and fed, and great credit is due to the men at the head of affairs who have been so successful in this undertaking. Apparently hon. gentlemen opposite are now taking up the time of Parliament with the object of driving the Government to the country, and if that is their wish, and if the Government should appeal to the country, these hon. gentlemen must expect very little sympathy

to-day. They realize that unless some help comes from countries such as Canada to assist them in producing the flax fibre for the purposes of their mills, they are going to be seriously handicapped. Representatives of these concerns have been in Canada during the past few months urging many of us who live in districts where flax grows extensively to try to have these mills started and some of their - products sent forward.
This year the whole Belgium export is cancelled, Germany has seized the whole stock of fibre, tow, yarns and linen. Germany having taken possession of the straw of the 1913 crop, held in reserve, and of the 1914 crop, harvested just before the war broke out and not marketed, there will De no flax sown this spring. For these reasons Belgium is out of the flax supply for three years.
This would appear to me to be Canada's opportunity. The improved methods used in handling the flax has made it a very profitable industry for the farmers. Pulling machines have been successful and the latest method of retting and caring for the flax have been the means of reducing the cost of handling to an enormous extent. The cotton industry of the southern States has tried to place the growing of flax in as much disfavour as possible. Canada cannot ever become great in cotton; she can become great in flax. If proper assistance is given 1 look forward not only to the old mills being operated, but to large mills being established in the Northwest as part of an industry which will add materially to the agricultural wealth of Canada.
I believe that a small commission should be appointed at the earliest possible date whose duty it should be to send out literature from time to time to men interested in flax. That commission should visit the mills which have'not been operated and induce them to reopen, and should see to it that sufficient seed is placed at their disposal at a reasonable price. Other duties of that commission would be: to visit each mill once at seeding time, harvesting, spreading, retting and turning, in order that they might obtain the best results; to see that the best of seed is used for planting purposes; to see to the proper grading of flax fibre for export; to investigate the new means of retting which are being introduced from time to time; to start the flax industry again in the province of Quebec if possible; to keep posted in the new European methods of handling flax; to find out ways and means of disposing of flax [Mr. J. E. Armstrong. 5
and its by-products in Canada; to assist the flax growers to co-operate with others in the importation of flaxseed from Holland; to devise some means whereby flax grown and scutched by the farmers on the farm in small quantities can be marketed to advantage; to devise a plan to settle disputes between the farmer and the flax buyer in regard to prices and to the standardization of flax both as to seed and to fibre. New Canadian strains should be developed; encouragement should be given in the way of baling the crop; lower freight rates should be secured; information concerning tests as to the exhaustiveness of flax on the soil should be disseminated. The farmers should be disabused of any prejudice they may have against flax growing, and if possible the establishment of paper mills in flaxseed centres should be encouraged in centres such as Saskatchewan where coarse straw can be profitably utilized. The United States, Ireland, Holland, France and other countries should be visited to inquire into and study their methods of treating flax. In short, every possible assistance should be rendered toward the development of this industry. I hope the Government will give immediate attention to this matter and that some assistance will be forthcoming.
In conclusion, I wish to congratulate this Government on the Budget and to say that it is a reasonable, fair, businesslike proposition, and that I have every confidence in the good sense and business management of the Prime Minister and his advisers.

Mr. Speaker, it is a good thing that the hon.
[DOT] member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) came to his " in conclusion," for up to that point the hon. gentleman had not mentioned the Budget. He took us through the history of the Liberal Administration from 1896; he spoke of dreadnoughts, of flax, of loyalty -of everything except the question which is now an issue between the two parties sitting in this House. I intend first to take up briefly the points that have been raised by my hon. friend. In the first place, he found fault with the hon. member for St. John City (Mr. Pugsley) for his attitude on revotes, and said that when that lion, gentleman was Minister of Public Works in 1908 there were a number of revotes. The hon. member for St. John City did not say that money should not be revoted, but he objects to revotes that involve extra taxation. The revotes of 1908 did not mean extra taxation laid upon the people. The hon. member for

Lambton goes on to say that the Opposition is embarrassing the Government while our boys are marching to tlhe front. But the Opposition has declared that it is ready to Vote any amount of money asked by this Government to go on with the war. I do not- see how we can be charged with embarrassing the Government in the conduct -of the war. Being willing to help the Government all along, it is nothing but right that we should criticise what we think is -open to criticism. Otherwise, what was the reason for convening Parliament? The Government, having a majority in this House, has the duty of keeping the business of the country going, and they must take the responsibility of their actions. If the Opposition find that the manner in which the Government is fulfilling its duty is not according to what is right, it is their duty to criticise. But we do not want to embarrass -the Government on account of the war-not at all; and we shall prove it before the debate is over.
The hon. member for East Lambton raised a question which ought to be settled at once for all. He said to the Opposition: If you are anxious for a fight, if you want to have an election, you may have it immediately. It is just as well that we should understand each other in this regard.

I know that my hon. friend does not intend to misquote what I said. I did not use the word " immediately." I said that if hon. gentlemen wanted an election, it was up to this Government to pitch its tent right here and fight the matter out, and that if we could not convince hon. gentlemen opposite that they are in the wrong and we are in the right, the best thing to do would be to go to the country.

I have no objection to the correction of my hon. friend. He made two allusions to that subject during the course of his speech: first, I understood him to say that if we were anxious for a fight- the Government should pitch their tent and fight to a finish. Secondly, he said that if the Liberal party wanted an election, we should go to the country. That is what I understood him to say, and I think the explanation he has made beats that out. We are not ovjr anxious to have .an election, but if the Gv vernment wants it, it will find us ready to face it.
The hon. member asks what the Government of the day did in 1907, when we were
in the midst of a crisis. The Government of the day reduced its expenditure, while the Government of to-day is increasing its expenditure, that is the difference. We are opposed to the Government on this question of taxation, because they are increasing expenditures as well as increasing the burdens which have to be borne by the people.
My hon. friend says that every country is enlarging its public debt. To this assertion we do not object. When the Government at the war session asked us to vote $50,000,000, we voted the amount willingly. This year, when they ask for $100,000,000, we are ready to vote it without objection. We realize that this war in which our country is involved must increase the public debt. We are willing to shoulder part of the responsibility for the expansion of the debt, but we do not wish to be held responsible for the extra taxation that is to be imposed upon the people in a manner to which we take objection.
My hon. friend said that instead of building the Transcontinental the previous Government should have extended the Intercolonial to the coast. Having regard to the statistics concerning the Intercolonial at the present time, I think my hon. friend will realize that if the Intercolonial railway had been extended to the coast, the results would have been much less advantageous than thos^ which will be obtained by the construction of the Transcontinental, which is built by a private corporation.
My hon. friend compares the price of wheat in Winnipeg with the price of wheat in Minneapolis. It is all very well to speak of a home market, but what is the use of having a quotation from the Winnipeg market and not having a consumer for the produce that is put on that market? I would rather have the consumer than the quotation.
The hon. gentleman sought to draw a parallel between the action of the Government in connection with the proposed contribution- of $35,000,000 to the British Admiralty and the position of the present Administration in connection with the Budget. He said that the Government acted under the direction of the British Admiralty when they asked Parliament to vote $35,000,000 for the Mother Country. Evidently my hon. friend desires to intimate that this Budget of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance has been drawn under the direction of the Admiralty. I think it is not fair that the Admiralty should be held responsible for anything the responsi-

bility for which rests upon the Government.
My hon. friend says that in respect of the $50,000,000 which have been voted, and the $100,000,000 which are being appropriated for war purposes, the Opposition did not and would not dare vote against the Government. I am not a scholar in the English language, and very often when a new word comes up in this House I go to the library and consult dictionaries and lexicons for the purpose of finding out the meaning of the word so employed. I have heard an hon. member in this House read an extract carefully prepared upon the words obsolete and obsolescent, and contend that the ships, which would have been tendered for under the Naval Act of 1910, would have been obsolete tne moment the contract was granted. But quite recently the Government bought two submarines which had been rejected by the Government for which they were ordered; they paid for them $250,000, and they were not obsolete. It is the same with the extra-superfine distinction between the two words "false" and "untrue." The same applies to the word "truce." The two parties have entered into a truce which, according to the dictionary, is a cessation of hostilities. Listening as you do, Mr. Speaker, with careful attention to the speeches which are delivered in this House, would you believe, after having heard the speech which has just been delivered by the hon. member for East Lamb-ton, that the party to which he belongs has entered into a truce and has ceased hostilities? When the two parties entered into a truce, the right hon. leader of the Opposition gave the Government a free hand in the direction of the affairs of this country. Parliament was summoned; the Government asked for a certain amount of money; we granted it willingly. All proposed amendments to existing laws which were suggested by the Government were willingly supported by the Opposition. When the session was over it was suggested that a Ereneh-Canadian regiment be formed in the province of Quebec. My right hon. friend and leader went on the public platform with his old political opponent and asked the young men to enlist, and the formation of a regiment was completed inside of three weeks. Would you be surprised to know, Sir, that at that very moment, when my right hon. friend and leader was respecting the truce which had been declared between the two parties, our friends of the Conservative party were circulating literature and cartoons with the professed object of preparing for an election, which, it was alleged, would be held on November 28, 1914?
In the province of Quebec?

It seems to me but fitting that my first words spoken in this House should bear reference to the loss which this Parliament has suffered in the death of the gentleman who preceded me in the position which I now occupy. The more I have come in contact with the members of this House and heard their references to the late hon,
9 p.m. Mr. Clare the more I have been impressed with the high place which he occupied in the estimation and the affections of the men with whom he was associated here. In his home town of Preston the splendid industries with which he was identified stand as a monument to his ability as a business man. We in South Waterloo who knew him so well feel that so great was the work in which he was engaged and so widespread his influence throughout Canada that his loss may well be referred to as a national one.
I	should also like to give expression on this occasion to the very great pride and pleasure that I feel at being permitted to serve in this House under the gentleman who occupies the high position of Premier of this Dominion of Canada. For ten years he was the chosen leader of his party while in Opposition. For more than three years he has been Premier of this country, during which time Canada has passed through perhaps the most difficrflt period in her history. I believe it is the verdict of the people of Canada to-day, and will be the verdict of the people more than ever in the future, that by the statesmanlike manner in which he has guided this country through this difficult time, the Premier has measured up to the best traditions of British statesmanship, and his place is secure in the honour roll of great Canadians.
The hon. member for St. Hyaeinthe (Mr. Gauthier) who has just resumed his seat will pardon me if I do not follow in detail the various arguments he has advanced, but there are one or two points to w'hich I shall refer. It has seemed to me as I have followed this debate, that after the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) had spoken for the gentlemen opposite,

the field that has been covered since that time has been practically the same ground over and over again. I should just like to refer to one of the points that was made by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat, a point that was also emphasized very emphatically by the hon. member foist. John (Mr. Pugsley) this afternoon; and that is their insistence that the Government of the day should cut down expenditures. I confess, Mr. Speaker, that I have a very limited knowledge of the procedure followed by this House in the carrying on of its business, but it does seem to me that it would be a much more businesslike proceeding if hon. gentlemen opposite, instead of speaking in a general way about expenditures, would wait until the Estimates are before the House and then tell us which of them they object to.
The hon. member for St. Hyaeinthe (Mr. Gauthier) also stated that the great burden of taxation in this Budget fell upon the people who were least able to bear it. Well, the Bank of Montreal, under this new taxation system, will pay into the treasury of this country $150,000 per annum, the Bank of Commerce $135,000 per annum, and the Imperial Bank $60,000 per annum, and the other banks will pay in like proportion. On the day following that on which the Minister of Finance brought down 'his Budget, I was in the office of the general manager of a bank in the oity of Toronto, and he said to me: Our share of this taxation will be $60,000 a year, but the banks will not attempt to shift that burden on to their customers, with whom they have been doing business, but will cheerfully pay dt, feeling that they are discharging a patriotic obligation which they owe to Canada and to the Empire. That, Sir, I have no doubt, represents the feeling amongst the banking institutions of this country.
I represent a constituency, important from an agricultural standpoint and important also from an industrial standpoint, and my constituents aTe intelligent people, who follow closely the discussion of public affairs, and I want to tell the Minister of Finance that I have not, up to the present, received a single complaint from them against the customs .tariff as proposed in this war Budget.
I can compliment the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) on the manner in which he handled his subject in criticising the Budget, and \ have found that the hon. gentlemen on his side of the House who have spoken since he did

have done him the compliment of largely following his argument. As I understand the position which the hon. gentleman and his party take with regard to this Budget, it is, that if the gentlemen who have been in charge of tire affairs of this country during -the past three years had been more careful in their expenditure, and had husbanded better the revenues of the country, there would have been no need for a war Budget. Well, the people of Canada know, the people of the world know, that as a consequence of this war the business and financial conditions of the world have been revolutionized, and that in every country, whether warring or neutral, it has been necessary to introduce unusual fiscal measures of the kind we are now discussing. In the neutral United States, which is far removed from the seat of conflict, shortly after the war broke out it became necessary to introduce special legislation to take care of the financial situation. Australia, New Zealand, every civilized country, has had to pass special legislation to meet the extraordinary conditions which have arisen. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) says: Had 1 been Minister of Finance during the past three years, and had I had surrounding me on the Treasury benches my chosen people, I would have so administered the financial affairs of Canada that it would not have been necessary to introduce any war Budget. 1 must admit that for the short time I have been in this House I have been very much impressed with the ability of the hon. gentleman (Mr. A. K. Maclean), but when he makes a contention of that kind, I feel I cannot pay equal tribute to his modesty. When the Liberal party in the Dominion advances such an argument, I am forced to think that the people of Canada will not be prepared to take them as seriously as they themselves.
Another point raised by the financial critic of the Liberal party was that these proposed changes in the tariff made the tariff so high that it became prohibitive, and that it would consequently restrict trade. I have no doubt that hon. gentlemen opposite are sincere when they say that this will be a high (tariff, and perhaps they are sincere when they say it will restrict trade, but I certainly cannot agree with them in the conclusion they have arrived at in this respect. Let them look at the tariff which has been in force in the United States for the last twenty-five years, and let them average the duties of that tariff and then compare that average with
the average duties in the war Budget now submitted by the Minister of Finance, and they will find that the average rate of duty in the United States has been considerably higher than the average rate in this proposed war Budget. And, Sir, I do not think it can be successfully contended that the tariff in the United States has not always supplied an abounding revenue for the needs of that country.
Particular stress has been laid by hon. gentlemen opposite on the changes proposed *in the tariff with reference to the British preference. They say that under no circumstances would they touch the British preference, but I can tell them that if they occupied the Government benches to-day, and if they were to add that seven and a half per cent duty on raw materials and leave the British preference as it is, it would be a very serious thing indeed for Canadian industries. There are in my constituency a number of woollen mills, and they are owned by gentlemen, some of whom support the party opposite, but I want to tell those gentlemen on the other side of the House, that if they adopted such a policy as they propose they would adopt, it would not be very favourably received by that army of people who are engaged in our woollen industries. I submit further, Mr. Speaker, that in so far as the principle of the British preference is concerned, it remains unchanged by this Budget.
A great deal has been said by hon. gentlemen opposite about extravagant expenditure, and while I have no desire to weary the House by an array of figures, I would like to refer to four items of expenditure which this Government had to undertake during the last three years. During the short time the present Government have been in power they, paid $56,000,000 towards the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, $10,000,000 for the Quebec bridge, $38,000,000 to the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, which they "were obliged to pay under an interpretation of the Grand Trunk Pacific agreement, made by the Liberal Government, and $15,000,000 to prevent the Grand Trunk Pacific from being tied up in 1913. Here we have a total of $119,000,000 which had to be paid by this Government, and every dollar of which is a legacy from the Liberal Government and an obligation incurred by them which the present Government had to assume. I have no doubt that were I thoroughly to analyse the situation I would find other large sums of a like nature.
I would like for a moment to refer to a

matter brought up by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) in the part which he took in this debate the other night. The hon. member said that he would like to see a more equitable distribution of the taxes than the new customs tariff would give, and he advocated direct taxation. The Minister of Finance has introduced no new principles in his War Budget; he has simply extended the principles that have always underlain the customs tariff. Those same principles were in effect in the tariff that was in operation in this country between the years 1896 and 1911. In so far as my knowledge goes, I have never heard that the hon. member for Edmonton tried to induce the party with which he is identified to change from a customs tariff to a system of direct taxation.
The hon. member for Edmonton also said that the duties on lumber, cement and many other articles, to which I need not refer, affected the prairie provinces. It has been my privilege to visit the provinces of the West; and if I were to be asked what is the chief characteristics of the people of the West, my answer might well be that one of their chief characteristics is their deep-rooted loyalty to Canada and to the Empire. When the hon. member for Edmonton says that the people of the West will be affected by these taxes, if I know the spirit of the people of the West, I say that they want to be affected by these taxes, because they realize that when they are so affected, they are paying a patriotic debt which they owe to Canada and to the Empire.
Reference has also been made by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House to the made-in-Canada campaign, and hon. gentlemen opposite have been inclined to hold it up to ridicule. I do not think that hon. gentlemen opposite properly appreciate the significance of this made-in-Canada campaign. What does it mean? Made in Canada means employment to Canadian industry. When our industries are busy and when our people are well employed, the Minister of Finance of to-day or the minister of to-morrow, whoever he may be, need not worry about the revenues of this country.
The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark), not in this debate but on another occasion-and 1 followed his remarks with a great deal- of interest-also paid his compliments to this made-in-Canada idea. His statement was that he was sorry to see this Government give its approval to it; that

it savoured to him too much of the iuea of " made in Germany," and that in so far as he was concerned, he was too good a Britisher to have anything to do with it. My prejudices against Germany do not carry me as iar as that. The Canadian people have a great deal to learn from the German people. It will be a great thing for this country when our people have the same efficiency in all the walks of l:fe that Germany has been able to instil into her people. We have also very much to learn from Germany in matters of education as applied to industry and also to agriculture. Canada cannot do better than take as an example what has been accomplished during the last forty years by the German empire. The development and growth of Germany can to a very large extent be attributed to the great assistance which she has received in the convenient open market which she has had, the free trade market of Great Britain. As a result of that great trade with Great Bn ain, the greatest market in the world, Germany has developed until she has become one of the greatest and most powerful nations in the world.
The point I would like to make is this,' that what the German empire has done the Dominion of Canada in the future ought to be able to do. Compare for a moment the opportunities of the two countries. We have room here for sixteen German empires. German soil is not as rich as our own. The Germans ..have not the great wealth of forests such as we possess; they have not the great lakes for inland shipping; they have not sea coasts such as we possess; and yet we see what has been accomplished by Germany. As a result of this war, new trade routes will be built up; new business connections in the old land will be developed in a way never before known; but the empire to which we belong, whatever changes there may be; will come out of this struggle with a greater standing in the world and a greater influence for good amongst the nations than she has ever befqre possessed. With those changed conditions, a splendid field of opportunity is offered not only for colonial, but for British statesmen. If Great Britain, with the great trade which she will command in the future, is going to build up another giant, tnat giant should come from people of her own breed, it should spring from a people who ask no better future, for no nobler destiny than that they may ibe permitted to work

out their future as part of the British Empire.
So, it seems to me, the future promises a great opportunity for Canada, an opportunity to which our public men, our statesmen, should direct attention. Right Hon. David Lloyd George, Chancellor of the Exchequer, stated the other day that the cost of this war to Great Britain for the first year amounted to $2,500,000,000. An enormous debt will have to be assumed by the people of the Motherland. We know that a large part of the people of the Motherland have expressed themselves as being in favour of tariff reform and preferential trade. Now, my thought is this-tha't, as a result of the piling up of this debt and of the period of reconstruction which will follow, Great Britain will be compelled to adopt a customs tariff again; and when that time comes it should be the duty of not only Canadian but British statemen to see to it that there shall be secured for the products of Canada a preference in that market; and I know of nothing that will do more than such a preference to promote the welfare, the progress and the development of the Dominion.
I feel that I should not longer trespass on the patience of this House. I was told that when a new member rises for the first time in his place he is received in a very considerate way. That has been my own experience, and I must thank hon. members for the indulgent way in which they have received my efforts.

I congratulate the hon. member for South Waterloo- (Mr. Scott) on his maiden effort. I am sure we all' must acknowledge that his speech in dignity and ability was all that we could expect. I join in his expressions of regret at the death of Ms predecessor, Mr. Clare. I am sure that we on this -side regret that gentleman's death as much as do hon. gentlemen on the other side, foir he was a very capable man, a man who had risen in the world by his own efforts, and who had proven himself a man in every respect.
I will not attempt to criticise my hon. friend's speech particularly, but I wish to offer one or two remarks upon it. He started out by telling us that if we would oppose the votes in the Estimates we should be doing our duty more than by criticising the Budget. When he has been longer a- member of this House he will know that we do oppose many of the votes in the Estimates-and that is all the good 38	*
it does. The hon. gentleman says that the banks are ready to pay the extra taxation laid upon them by the Budget. But these are public corporations and the individuals who control their operation do not pay a cent of this taxation out of their own pockets. Moreover, if that taxation becomes a burden on the banks they will simply charge it up to us poor devils who have to borrow money. That is human nature, of course; but it does not show loyalty or patriotism on the part of the banks. They are prepared to do their duty, no doubt; 1 am not saying anything against them; I shall have occasion to mention them later in my remarks.
The hon. gentleman says the whole business community is feeling the hard times brought on by the war. in his own town, as in many other towns in this Dominion, if it were not for the war-and I am sorry to give that as a reason; it is an unspeakable. reason-the hard times would be a hundred per cent worse than they are to-day.
Don't you believe that.

I not only believe it,
but know it; and in the constituency of my hon. triend who has just spoken I think they have contracts for shells out of which they make money. They do not make shells, woollens, and other goods for nothing, even for the Imperial Government. And so it is with many kinds of industries throughout this Dominion. Everybody knew these hard times were coming. The Minister of Finance warned us of them a year ago. I will go into that also later on. The hon. member for South Waterloo mentioned the woollen industries and said they could not stand the increased duty on the raw material unless the duty on the finished goods were also increased. 1 cannot agree with him. I know something about the woollen industry, in the same torm as do the people in his own town-knitted goods-and I do not agree that the industry could not have stood an increase on the raw material. But we have been opposed to increased duties not only on the raw material but also on the finished article. The hon. junior member of Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) has told you distinctly that we were opposed to the increase of duties entirely'.
The hon. member for South Waterloo tells us that Great Britain will be compelled to adopt a customs tariff when this war is over. As I do not have anything to do with the management of Great Britain's affairs, and as I find that the Cabinet in

nue producing tariff. I shall not suggest that the tariff is being enacted for the purpose of assisting, as some of my friends say, the large corporations or the manufacturers. I shall not suggest anything of that kind, but I am going to say that as far as I know business the tariff will not be a revenue producing tariff. I believe there would have been a greater revenue from the tariff as it was before than will be derived from the tariff as it is. now, for the simple reason that on a great many articles the tariff is absolutely prohibitive. You take the one article of woollens. The Finance Minister said that he relieved the people who could not afford to bear the burden to a great extent. There is nobody who can afford it or who cannot afford but is forced to wear woollens in some manner or form. Practically all the clothes we wear in the winter are woollen or should be, and axe to the extent of our power to insure their being woollen, so that every man, poor or rich, is taxed on this article. The tariff on woollens is raised from 35 per cent to 42J per cent. Heaven knows that the man who cannot do business with a protection of 35 per cent should go out of business, there is no doubt about that. The tariff on cotton is also increased to a ridiculous extent, and so it is on such things as flannel and worsted and all manner of wearing apparel, which all the people of this country must get, for even if they wanted to go naked they could not because it is too cold most of the time. There is the difference between a revenue tariff and a protective tariff:	My hon.
friends on the other side of the House have always twitted us on -this side that when we were in power we always kept up the duty; but I want to say that the inclination during all the time that the Liberal party were in pow'er, led by my right -hon. friend and leader, the inclination was downwards and the inclination to place more things on the free list was always there. We were increasing the free list every time. I counted the other night the articles in the old tariff that were on the free list and found there were 232. But in the tariff now brought down there are only about 100 articles on the free list that were on before. That is where we are going to feel the burden to a large extent. Let me mention one other article of interest to the farmer, of whom we are all talking more or less. He will have to pay 7^ per cent duty on number 9 and number 12 wire, or the wires that were free before, 
out of which fence is manufactured. There is hardly a farmer in Canada, either west or east, who does not have to buy wire fencing. There is not a farmex in Canada but will have to buy wire fencing because the old fences have largely gone to pieces. The Minister of Finance is charging the farmer in that one item about $175,000, if you take last year's importation as a basis. The farmer will be caused gome regret if you raise the price of his fence somewhere in the neighbourhood of $3 per ton. My hon. friend might say that the farmer can buy his wire here. There is not the slightest fear but what the one or two industries that do draw wire in this country will raise the price of their wire to the utmost 'that they will be allowed to by the duty that is now imposed. There is no possible doubt about that, because they have been supplying very little of the wire	used	in Canada.
I am not taking into account the wire used in the telegraph and telephone industries, and similar businesses. The wire to farmers alone will cost in the neighbourhood of from $175,000 to $200,000 if they use as much in the coming year as they did in 1914. And that brings me to what my hon. friend the junior member for Halifax has said we should do with the tariff this year. Hon. members on the other side of the House are inclined to laugh at our suggestion that the expenditure be curtailed. The first item I am going to speak about is the expenditure on the Hudson Bay railway. I know that my hon. friends on this side of the House promised to build that railway, but I have come to the conclusion, or almost come to the conclusion, that political parties are justified in certain instances in not keeping promises which they should never have made. My hon. friends on this side of the House have this virtue, that while they promised to start the Hudson Bay railway, they never did. They sent out surveyors and got reports on the route whicn, however, were not encouraging enough to induce them to start building.
Mr. SAM. SHARPE: Did they not let the first contract?

Not that I know of. At any rate they did not build any of the road. The Government are asking this year for a vote of $5,500,000 for the Hudson Bay railway. The hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) the other evening said that that could be cut down to $1,000,000 without hurting anybody. I say it could be

absolutely wiped out, and that if the Government of the day would pull up the rails and sell them to somebody else for whatever they would bring, they would earn the lasting gratitude of the people of this country. In my judgment the Hudson Bay railway has no more chance of earning money than Stefansson would have if he built a railway upon one of those islands where he is lost. They do say that there are some fish in Hudson bay. That could easily be proved, and if there are any fish there and we wished to sell them, the best possible way and the only reasonable way would be to extend the Timiskaming and Northern Ontario railway to some point on James bay, and the fish could then be brought out to the Transcontinental and transferred east and west to the great cities that would consume it. The reports that I have read of the country between Le Pas and Port Nelson show that there is certainly nothing else to bring out from that country unless they bring out the frozen ground once a year or so. We could make a saving of $5,500,000 on that item alone. My hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) has mentioned public buildings in Ontario.
What is the hon. gentleman's view as to stopping the work on the Welland canal?
I would not stop the work, but you could easily reduce the expenditure on the canal this year, as you could all necessary expenditures.
I think the contracts are all let, with one exception. Which one would you stop?

My hon. friend knows that there is a vast difference between pushing on a work and letting it progress at a reasonable rate. My hon. friend knows it is not necessary to stop the contracts. A great many men were sent out of this country last fall. Somebody said just now, 100,000, but I believe it is nearer 50,000; at any rate most of the soldiers were working men, and their absence makes a great difference in the number of working men in this country. My hon. friend knows that the Government could ease up on the expenditure both at St. John and on the Welland canal, and on any other proper public works in this country, and thereby save several million dollars without doing anybody any harm. Now as to public buildings in Ontario. I see in the Estimates that $3,905,100 is required for .this purpose. My hon. friend
the other night said he would cut off $1,500,000 of that. I would cut off $3,000,000, and not a particle of harm would be done to anybody. There are a number of buildings here that are absolutely unnecessary to the towns that are supposed to require
them.	What would any business man do in our position? What could he do but curtail his expenditure and cut his coat according to his cloth, as the old saying is? Why,
then,	should not the Government do that?
Why should we not, as representing the people of this country, do what the people want?	Take the Barrie drill hall, for
instance. There is no more need of a drill hall at Barrie at the present time than there is of one in Palestine. Nor does Berlin need another public building to accommodate the public. There is the Brantford drill hall. Good gracious, are we never to be done with Brantford? Within the last two years $275,000 was spent on a public building there, and now they wan,t a drill hall at a cost of $75,000. We all know that drill halls are absolutely unnecessary this year, for practically no drills will take place. The Militia Department has cut out its annual vote for drilling, and quite properly, because the men who are going to the front are drilling together in different sections all over the country. We have found out that it is not
drilling up and down a drill hall 10 p.m. that makes a soldier. A soidjer
should be drilled out in the open weather and given some exercise. Even I myself find it necessary to go out after six o'clock for a walk of two or three miles, in order to keep myself alive after sitting here all day. Soldiers would be better if not drilled in drill halls. Some hon. gentlemen say that these drill halls are also used for Fat Stock shows. Well, let them hold the Fat Stock show in somebody's barn this year. It will not hurt them any. Colling-wood also wants a public building at a cost of $35,000, and here is a drill hall for Galt at $45,000. I have no doubt that the hon. gentleman wiho has just spoken would be glad to get that building in Galt, but the little bit of money that is spent in these towns does not do the general country any good. It does not do the good that would be done if the money was kept in the treasury or went to pay our debts, and it is the general good of the country that we are supposed to look after, not some individual who may get a few votes by our spending money in his constituency.
There is an appropriation for a building at Burford, I believe. What does my hon. friend think of that?
Yes, J2*,000. I think it is a ridiculous expense.
The village of Burford is in the constituency I represent, or that I endeavour to represent.
You represent it well. That is all right.

Is my hon. friend aware that the villages of Drumbo and Princeton in the constituency that he represents, neither one of which is as large or important or progressive as Burford, are asking for public buildings?

I am aware of the fact that last year the village of Princeton, after seeing the example set by the village of Burford, came down here and asked for a public building. I am also aware of the fact that they asked for a builamg to cost only $5,000. I am also aware of the fact that there is a vote here of $25,000 for a building in Burford.
I am also aware that the revenue from the village of Plattsville is greater than the revenue from the village of Burford, I am also aware that the revenue from the village of Drumbo is greater than the revenue from Burford, I am also aware that the village of Plattsville is a much better village than the village of Burford, and I am aware of the, fact that these villages were satisfied with the expenditure of $5,000. I am further aware, that if you put a building worth five or six thousand dollars in the village of Burford, it would be a palace alongside the rest of the buildings there.

Is the hon. gentleman
aware that the village of Drumbo algo asked for a public building?
I told you I did.
You are then aware that both places have asked for a public building?
Yes.
Are you aware they have asked the member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) and myself to intercede for them ?
1 am not aware of that; they did not show good taste there.
Does the hon. gentleman know that the village of Princeton revised its estimate as to what kind of a public building it wanted and that it now thinks it should have one costing $15,000?
I did not know that.
Well, that is the fact. Let me put this last question to my hon. friend -is he in favour or is he opposed to public buildings for the villages of Princeton and Drumbo? .

Ever since I have had a seat in this House I have expressed myself in favour of the principle of erecting public buildings for the purpose of collecting revenue in towns and cities throughout the country, in proportion to the revenues collected in these various places. I am stating to-night that I am opposed to these buildings being erected this year when the revenue is short, and I am stating to-niuht that if you want to build a house, Mr. Representative for Brant, and you have not the money and cannot borrow it, you cannot build the house, and the Government should be guided by the same principle identically. I repeat that I am absolutely in favour of erecting public buildings for the purpose of collecting revenue, in proportion to the revenue collected in each place, but I am not in favour of erecting a $25,000 building and putting a caretaker into it in a village like Burford, where the revenue is about $1,200 a year, and in view of the fact that the revenue is being collected now for an expenditure of probably three or four hundred dollars a year. I have not looked up the post office returns to-night to see what the revenue or expenditure in Burford is, but it is in the neighbourhood of the figures I have given. The expenditure on public buildings in the province of Ontario could be cut down, at the lowest calculation, $3,000,000 this year, without hurting anybody. We should wait for another year to see how the revenue will be then. I do not know anything about the province of Quebec in that respect, but I have not the slightest doubt that the expenditure for public buildings in all the other provinces could be proportionately cut down. Then take the Trent Valley canal, for which there is a vote of one million or one million and a half dollars this year, and I am quite sure that those people who go-out on picnic parties on the Trent Valley canal could, for the year to come, do so by motor, or rig, or walk. All they do on that canal is to hold picnic parties up and down, and therefore that

million and a half dollars to be expended there could be saved for this year.
Does the hon. member know what the depth of the Trent Valley canal is, and the size of the locks?
The depth on the sills is seven feet, I think.

It is eight feet two
inches.

Leave out the two inches;
I think on most of it you will get nearer to seven feet than eight feet.
It is deep enough to cost a lot of money.

Yes, it is deep enough
to pour a lot of money into it. There is no transportation waiting on the expenditure there and nothing would be hurt by waiting and saving that million and a half dollars for the coming year. Then as to the French river; I asked the Minister of Public Works last year what he is going to do about the French river, and he said he did not, know, and I do not believe he knows yet, but everybody knows that to put a canal on the French river would be 'an absolute waste of money. I suppose there are a lot of people in this country who still in their imagination, fortified imagination I would call it, think we would be justified in going on with the expenditure on the Georgian Bay Canal. I am glad to say these people are scarce, because it would be a wilder and more foolish expenditure that the expenditure on the Hudson Bay Railway.
Mr. GERALD V. WHITE: What stand does the right hon. leader of my hon. friend take on that?

It does not make any
difference to me what stand my leader takes on it; I am telling you what I think about it,' and I am only speaking for myself. There was only one possible object in building the Hudson Bay railway and that was to cheapen'transportation for the grain of the West, but how are you going to cheapen transportation when you have to haul that grain there and build elevators and store it from one year to the other. Any one who buys grain knows that when you have to carry it over for a year and pay interest charges you cannot get any benefit from cheaper transportation for the grain. Then, when you have got the grain at Hudson Bay you have to nave a line of steamers to take it out and there is not a man living wlip would invest a dollar in a
line of steamers which would work for three months of the year and lie idle for the other nine months. That is the plain fact about the Hudson Bay railway, and the Georgian Bay Canal would be a thousand times worse if that could be possible.
Hon. gentlemen opposite talk about throwing men out of work. There is no necessity to throw men out of work. These great enterprises, such as the Welland Canal, the Quebec Bridge, the improvements at St. John, N.B., can be gone on with in a reasonable way, and they will afford employment. The railways will have to make improvements and they will at least have to attend to the upkeep of their roads, and there is no fear of men being thrown out of work. When spring comes there will be lots of work for every one jto do. We are now preaching from end to end of the land patriotism and production, while at the same time we are at every turn, by this new tariff, making the necessaries of life dearer for the men who have to produce, and we are making it harder every day for the farmer to get a fair profit from the results of his toil.
Many people believe that the farmers are making fortunes. There is not a cent of profit in farming at the present day unless a farmer has grain to sell, and there are not many farmers in Ontario that I know of that have any grain to sell. The men who have grain to sell are making a great deal of money, but the men who are raising cattle and hogs at the present price of grain are not making any money.
Not only does this new tariff not help the people of the country to produce more, but it retards the production of the country in every way. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance could wipe out $30,000,000 of the expenditure of this country without the slightest difficulty and let the estimated revenue of next year meet the expenditure for that period. I hope that he will see his way to do so. I have great faith in my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, and I hope that he will not be influenced by his colleagues and by those who say, "dash away and spend the money," to go on with such a wild-goose proposition as this tariff and the expenditure that he proposes by this year's Estimates.

I
understand that the motion under which this debate is being conducted is for the House to go into Committee of Ways and Means, and that it is usual on an occasion -of this kind to consider the problem of the ways and means of the country. I have

followed the debate up to the present time with a considerable degree of attention and with a hope that we might hear from some of the members of the Opposition, whose right and proper duty it is to offer fair criticism, some constructive criticism, something: in the nature of a suggestion to help the Government to meet the most critical financial period with which the country has probably ever been faced in its history; but up to the present moment I have failed to catch any constructive suggestion from hon. gentlemen opposite.
I desire to say a few words in reply to some of, the arguments presented by my hon. friend the member for North Oxford (Mr., Nesbitt). He seems to have based his arguments on this one proposition, namely, that the expenditures of the country for the forthcoming year should be reduced so as to meet the estimated revenue for that period. In fact, that seems to be the main argument adduced by hon. members opposite. It was rather interesting to observe the efforts of my hon. friend in wiggling his way through the Ontario Estimates. I was expecting him to criticise them at somewhat greater length; but the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Fisher), I think, rather upset him with some of the queries that he advanced.
The hon. member for North Oxford said that we should have cut off the further construction of the Hudson Bay railway at this time. Does he not remember that, when the right hon. the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) was Prime Minister of this country, and when he and his colleagues sat on this side of the House supporting him, they, in season and out of season, advocated the construction of the Hudson Bay railway? I was not a member of the House then; but I understand that my hon. friend supported and voted for that project.
I did not.
Did my hon. friend vote against it?
I never voted for it. I never heard it brought up.

That is very good indeed. The hon. member certainly supported the right hon. the leader of the Opposition when he was Prime Minister of this country, and in western Canada advanced the construction of the Hudson Bay railway as one of his main policies.
And they won their elections on it.

Moreover, on no occasion in the history of this House did my hon. friend raise his voice against this project. I challenge any hon. gentleman opposite to produce a single vote from that party against that project while they were in power. The Government of the day, composed of hon. gentlemen opposite, entered into a contract for the construction of that railway, and the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) himself signed the contract.

The then Solicitor
General says that I did not do so.
What does my hon. friend say?
I take his word.
Will the hon. gentleman deny that he signed the contract?
Whom would you rather believe?

I am bound to believe
the hon. gentleman's statement. In any case, this fact cannot be gainsaid, that our hon. friends opposite supported and advocated the project. They signed the first contract and entered into contracts for the construction of that railway. The construction has been carried out by this Government to the satisfaction of the people of the West, and I believe the railway will prove a very satisfactory project. The question of the construction of railways, of the opening up of the vast territory of the West, has always been a question of great difficulty and danger. You, Mr. Speaker, and the older members of the House who have had the honour of sitting here for many years, will remember that when the Canadian Pacific railway was constructed it was prophesied by certain learned gentlemen in this House and out of it that it would be an absolute failure. Within thirty years the Canadian Pacific Railway Company has grown to be one of the largest and most reputable corporations in the known world. As the Canadian Pacific railway has more than vindicated the confidence placed in it by the Canadian people at that time, and as nearly every other project of a similar character constructed in western Canada has proved itseslf to be a successful venture, it is reasonable for the people of Canada to believe that a railway to that inland sea of Hudson Bay will also be a success. At least we who live in western Canada have faith in the great West, and we believe that the railway will be a success. Let me call

my hon. friend's attention to certain resources. He speaks of moving carloads of frozen earth. It has been demonstrated, as far as it has been possible to investigate, that the Hudson Bay is a veritable storehouse of fish which will supply the food markets of Canada and of the world, because it must be remembered that to-day we are shipping from Prince Rupert clear to the old land frozen fresh fish, and the Hudson Bay is a very much nearer shipping place than is the western coast. Therefore in fish alone there are vast possibilities in that section of the country. We have also vast areas of pulp timber in that district, which commodity is rapidly becoming of more and more value in the Dominion and is supporting one of our most valuable industries, and for which the market is increasing day by day. Therefore, when hon. gentlemen suggest that the project should be cut off, that it is wasteful expenditure, that it is extravagantly unjustifiable on the part of the Government, they should at least be thoroughly seized of the facts of the case before they make such suggestions.
My hon. friend also suggested that certain portions of the Welland canal could be stopped. I am not familiar with the details of tine Welland canal other than this, that I know that a number of contracts have been entered into. The Government say-I shall be glad to be corrected if I am wrong -that no further contract shall be entered into in the immediate future, but that the present contracts shall be carried out.
I rise to correct the hon. gentleman. He says that I said that work on the Welland canal should be stopped. I distinctly stated that it should not be stopped.
I said that the hon. gentleman suggested that the work on the Welland canal should be greatly curtailed.
The hon. gentleman said I said it should be stopped.

I must again correct my hon. friend. I certainly never voted for an expenditure in Peterborough or Guelph such as he speaks about. I opposed such expenditures last year as I do this year. I did not enumerate all the places, but I opposed such expenditures generally.

These buildings were
put up by the late Government, and the hon. gentleman, so far as I am able to learn, did not once raise his voice in opposition to them. Now, a word as to the construction of drill halls which my hon. friend ridicules, and says that we are not using them and that men cannot be drilled in a hall. In every large city in Canada to-day, and in my own city particularly, we have to rent building after building to accommodate the contingents that we are raising. We have no drill hall except a very old one, in Vancouver, yet we need accommodation for the training of the men of these contingents, and so we are forced to rent buildings. If we had more drill halls in Canada where we could assemble the troops we are raising in all parts of the country and where we could give them the preliminary training and drill and then give them the mass drill in the cities where they are assembled, we should be better off.
The hon. gentleman took exception to the Trent Valley canal. That is a work that has been under way for a great many years and it is one that the people of Canada demand shall be completed and put into sue-

cessful operation at the earliest possible date. Parts of it are being operated now and, I am informed, with very great advantage to the country through which it passes. So with the Georgian Bay canal. Personally, I have never been very enthusiastic about that work, but I look upon it as a matter very largely affecting the people in the eastern part of Canada. The hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) would not object to that work going on. I think he would not say " Hear, hear! " to what his friend from North Oxford said. The hon. member for North Oxford said a moment ago unchallenged that he did not care for his leader or anybody else, that he was speaking for himself. It is a happy condition with these hon. gentlemen in the Opposition that they have the privilege of speaking for themselves without involving their party in the argument.
That is one of the beauties of being in opposition.

It reminds me that
possibly a great deal of the argument advanced within the last few days by hon. gentlemen is not-I was going to say is not quite sincere, but that wouid not be parliamentary; but what I mean to say is that many of the arguments on the question of expenditure are put possibly with the hope that the Government may be foolish enough to accept the advice and so injure themselves politically throughout the country. This Government could not possibly indulge in a more foolish act, in my estimation, than to curtail the expenditure on public works at this crisis in the history of the country. Now we have had very considerable criticism of the expenditures, and I shall ask the indulgence of the House for a few moments while we examine some of these expenditures. Because one of the things I have particularly remarked in this debate is that those hon. gentlemen who have criticised the Government fail, as my friend Mr. Joseph Martin puts it, to get down to brass tacks. While they offer criticisms, they do not show how improvement could be made. With regard to the increased expenditure we have certain items to which I wish to refer. First there is $8,730,000 in sinking fund. It' is utterly impossible for us to avoid the inclusion of that sum in our Estimates. I am possibly mistaken in what I thought I heard an hon. gentleman on the other side say this afternoon. But as I understood him he said that his view was that this sum should have been included in the sum we borrowed from the Mother Country to carry on 
the war. What are the facts? The Minister of Finance has made an arrangement with the Imperial Government, whereby all the moneys necessary for carrying on the war- that is war expenses and only war expenses -will be advanced on the general War Budget of the Old Land That is an arrangement for which the Finance Minister deserves a great deal of credit. It would be absurd for us to seek to include in those borrowings the interest covering the same. We get the money on most reasonable terms -the same rate that the Imperial Government will pay, which are the best rates in the world. And surely that is a sufficient concession. It has been argued that this is not a War Budget but that it is presented as a War Budget merely to cover up the failure of the Government to administer the affairs of the country aright. I wish to discuss for a moment the facts of the war with a view to showing hon. gentlemen opposite-though they do not need it; they know it already-that the conditions now pertaining are produced directly by the war, if not by this war, then by the. war of 1912. For we all remember that when the Balkan war broke out, and while it was raging, it was daily expected that the great powers of Europe would be dragged into the conflict in which we are to-day. The money interests of the world commenced hoarding funds against the possible outbreak for a period of two * years. And it is well they did so, well both for this country and for the Motherland. For I believe that if it had not been for the wisdom of Lloyd George, the great Finance Minister of the Old Land, Mr. Winston Cnurchill and others we should not have been in the happy position in which we are to-day, immune from attack by foreign countries.
In my city we have two lines of steamships, one of which is operated by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. Five steamships of this service, the Empress of Asia, the Empress of Russia-which are larger than any steamships running into Montreal-the Empress of China, the Empress of Japan and the Monteagle, were taken by the Admiralty a( the outbreak of the war and, with the exception of the Monteagle, which has been returned, are being used by them to-day. What effect did this have upon trade? It had this effect: we could not get bottoms in Vancouver for the export of goods, and the consequence was that export trade on the western coast was absolutely paralysed. Steamships not only of the Canadian Pacific railway lines but of

the Blue Funnel lines, the Harrison lines, the Holt and other lines, were taken over by the Admiralty, and the tonnage on the Pacific coast at Vancouver, at San Francisco, Portland, and other ports, became so scarce that freight rates were doubled. Today, therefore, we are precluded from export trade on the Pacific coast because of the lack of bottoms in which to carry our goods. Millions upon millions of dollars' worth' of lumber trade which is offering to our lumber men cannot be accepted because there is no way of transporting the goods. Yet Ihon. gentlemen opposite coolly stand up in their places in this House and, seemingly indifferent to their responsibilities as representatives of the people, say that the war is not the cause of the present disrupted conditions of trade and commerce in Canada.
Again, what effect has the absolute cutting off of all borrowings had upon our trade and commerce? First, the Federal Government could borrow no more money, except for the purposes which I have mentioned; secondly, all provincial borrowings were shut off, with the result that many public works were stopped. Municipal borrowings were suddenly cut off, and in my province-and, I believe, in other provinces as well-the provincial government was forced to come to the assistance of many municipalities in order that they might be enabled to carry out ordinary works throughout the coming year. Lastly, industrial borrowings were cut off and the activities of the various industries of the country were curtailed. This was directly attributable to the outbreak of this war in Europe.
The shutting off of borrowings directly affected the steel industry, because the carrying on of industrial and municipal works for which large amounts of money were borrowed involved the use of a considerable amount of steel. The steel industry was so seriously affected that factories at Hamilton and on the Atlantic coast were shut down, or almost shut down. The practical cessation of building operations throughout the whole of Canada is directly attributable to the outbreak of war. Large financial concerns wthich formerly received money from the old land were unable to secure any further amounts; loans could not be advanced on mortgages, buildings could not be erected; practically every industry was affected. I think every lion, gentleman opposite must admit that practically the whole of the stagnation in trade
which now prevails throughout Canada is directly attributable to the war.
Let us examine some of the items which have been criticised by hon. gentlemen opposite. What is the increase in respect of civil government? 3174,000, which consists of statutory increases authorized by legislation passed by the very hon. gentlemen who now criticise this item. What would they have us do? Because the revenue of a post office falls considerably during the year, would they have us close tne office and discharge the employees? The same applies to customs ports of entry. There has been an increase in the Post Office Estimates of $1,720,000. How is that increase being spent? Railway service, $405,000. That amount is devoted to parcel post. Up to the present time we have not begn able to receive the full benefit which is to be derived from the operation of the parcel post system, but would hon. gentlemen opposite suggest that this newly-organized branch of the postal service be dispensed with? Rural deliveries, an inci-ease of $350,-
000.	In 1912-13 600 new rural routes were established; in 1913-14, 940; to-day there are 2,857 routes. The establishment of these rural mail delivery routes is but the carrying *'out of the avowed policy of this Government during and prior to the last election. Hon. gentlemen opposite have stated that we are not carrying out our promises to the electors; here is a case in which the Government is faithfully carrying out one of its solemn pledges to the rural districts of Canada, yet hon. gentlemen opposite criticise the expenditure necessary to make good the word of the Government in that respect. In 1913-14 48,000 additional rural mail delivery boxes were established in the towns, villages and cities throughout the Dominion. These are a great convenience to the farmers of the country and to those living in the outlying districts.

Do the farmers not pay for their own boxes?
. Mr. STEVENS : I presume they do.
Tiien the Post Office Department obtains a revenue from that source; there is no expenditure.

My hon. friend knows that a postal service cannot be expanded without very considerable cost to the community. He knows, too, that the postal service of this or any other country is not looked upon as a means for obtaining revenue; it is looked upon as a means of

communication and a system of enabling the rural districts to keep in touch with the affairs of the world.	'

I think my hon. friend misunderstood me. He was quoting as an item of expense the number of rural mail delivery boxes that have been purchased by the Government. I was trying to point out that the farmers paid for these boxes; consequently there was no expenditure on the part of the Government.

My hon. friend misunderstands me; I am afraid I have not the faculty of making myself clear. We expended in the expansion of this postal service $1,721,000. I was trying to give to the House some evidence of the fact that the Government has done some real work in this connection. I will repeat my statement; the Government established in 1913, 600 new rural mail routes and in 1913-14, 940. They had in 1912-13, 23,000 rural mail delivery boxes; last year this number was increased to 48,000. The cost of the boxes was borne by those who obtained them, but the cost of the service was borne by the Government. I mention this to show that the Government has done its utmost to give the people of Canada an up-to-date postal service, and I think they have succeeded in doing so.
The Estimates for the Mounted Police have been increased by $509,000. Do hon. gentlemen opposite object to that? No body of men in any country in the world are more worthy of admiration and of the support of the people than the Mounted Police of Canada. The staff of this splendid body of men has been increased for the purpose of keeping track of subjects of the enemy who may be leaving or passing through or coming into the western country. Pensions are increased by $139,000, the statutory increase.
Then, we have subsidies to provinces, another statutory increase which must be given, for which the Government, the Minister of Finance is not responsible. It amounts to $192,000. In agriculture, there is an important increase. Our hon. friends say that this Government neglects the farmer. How is this being spent? One important item of expenditure is testing seed. One great cause of failure and weakness among the farming communities of Canada has been carelessness in the selection of seed; we all know that. During the recent years the present Government, under the able administration of the Minister of Agriculture, has been trying to assist the farmer in the selection of his seed and has
[Mr. Stevens.!
been testing it for him and helping him in every way. There have been increased expenditures in connection with the live-stock industry, and to enforce the Meats and Canned Foods Act. I have myself been impressing on the Government the necessity of increased vigilance in the inspection of canned fruits, meats, etc., and there have been great steps forward in this respect. There is also the Pest Act and the Fruit Branch. These are the items on which the money is being expended, and the increase is in each case thoroughly justifiable. The Government cannot carry out these works and keep their pledges unless they have some reasonable aid from the country in the [DOT] matter of their finances.
As the hour is late, I beg to move the adjournment of the debate.

Motion agreed to, and debate adjourned.
